seo.title: Google Ads Invalid Traffic Card: What It Shows
seo.meta_description: Google Ads now shows invalid traffic savings and credits in a new Overview card. What it means for Anaheim and Orange County advertisers and lead quality.

h1: Google Ads Invalid Traffic Card: See What Google Filters and Credits
answer: On November 12, 2026, Google began rolling out the Invalid Traffic Overview Card in Google Ads, which shows advertisers the amount saved by filtering invalid traffic and the credits issued for invalid activity found later. Google says it doesn't charge for invalid traffic. For Anaheim and Orange County advertisers, the card adds transparency, but lead quality still needs your own safeguards.
key_takeaways: Shows estimated savings and credited cost for invalid traffic.
Google says it doesn't charge for invalid traffic.
Google says it reduced exposure to invalid leads by an average of 30% so far in 2026.
Lead form protection is still the advertiser's job.

sections.heading: What Google announced
sections.body_html: On November 12, 2026, Keerat Sharma, Vice President and General Manager of Ads Privacy and Safety at Google, announced the Invalid Traffic Overview Card in Google Ads. Google says it gives advertisers front-end transparency into how it protects their campaigns. For the first time, businesses can see both the amount saved and the credits Google automatically provides for invalid activity.

sections.heading: What invalid traffic is
sections.body_html: Google's help page defines invalid traffic as traffic that doesn't represent genuine interest in your business. Its examples include non-human traffic from bots and automated software, accidental clicks caused by poor ad placement, fraudulent placements such as clickjacking and ad stacking, and intentional clicks from people with no genuine interest, such as competitors trying to raise your spend. Google notes the list isn't exhaustive.

sections.heading: You don't pay for it
sections.body_html: Google says it doesn't charge for invalid traffic. Invalid activity detected before the end of the billing cycle is removed from billing and campaign reports automatically. If it is detected after you were billed, Google issues a credit where appropriate and possible, shown as an Invalid activity adjustment on your invoice.

sections.heading: What the card shows
sections.body_html: Google's help page says the card, on the Overview page in the Campaigns menu, highlights two metrics for your selected date range: Estimated savings, the cost saved by automated protections, and Credited cost, the amount credited back for past invalid activity found after the billing period ended. Select View details for daily graphs, a breakdown by campaign and links to invoices with credits.

sections.heading: It's rolling out gradually
sections.body_html: Google notes the Invalid traffic card is rolling out gradually and may not be in your account yet. If you don't see it, check again over the coming weeks.

sections.heading: Other places to check
sections.body_html:
• Add the Invalid clicks column to your campaigns table to see clicks Google filtered out.
  • Check Billing, Summary, Adjustments for Invalid activity credits.
  • Use the Invalid Activity Credit Report in Report Editor to see metrics adjusted for credits.

sections.heading: Why filtered clicks and credits differ
sections.body_html: Google explains that you may see many filtered invalid clicks but small credit amounts, and that this is normal. The invalid clicks column shows traffic filtered before you were billed; credits cover invalid activity found after the billing cycle closed. The two numbers measure different things.

sections.heading: Invalid leads: a shared job
sections.body_html: Google says that so far in 2026 it has reduced advertiser exposure to invalid leads by an average of 30% through system upgrades. But its help page is clear that its filters can't block traffic from your site, and that some real people submit fake details. Lead quality is a shared effort: Google filters invalid traffic, and you protect your forms.

sections.heading: Protect your lead forms
sections.body_html:
1. Choose Leads as the campaign objective and optimize for goals such as qualified lead or booked appointment.
  2. Secure forms with tools like reCAPTCHA and server-side validation.
  3. Consider a double opt-in that confirms a real email address.
  4. Set up the Google tag and enhanced conversions to measure real customer actions.

sections.heading: If you suspect problems
sections.body_html: Google says you can request an investigation into invalid traffic within the last 60 days. Prepare your 10-digit customer ID, the exact dates, the campaign and ad group names, any suspicious keywords and your web server logs before you submit.

sections.heading: What this means for local advertisers
sections.body_html: For a roofer in Anaheim or a law firm in Santa Ana spending on Search ads, the card makes it easier to see that Google is filtering junk clicks. It doesn't tell you whether your leads turn into customers. Compare ad leads against your own records of booked jobs and signed clients.

sections.heading: A worked example
sections.body_html: Imagine an HVAC company in Orange that notices a run of form fills with fake phone numbers. The Invalid traffic card shows savings and a small credit, so Google is filtering some activity, but the fake forms keep arriving. The company adds reCAPTCHA and server-side checks to the form, switches its conversion goal to booked appointments and imports which leads became jobs. Fake submissions fall and the campaign optimizes toward real customers.

sections.heading: Ads and organic work together
sections.body_html: Paid search works best alongside a strong organic presence. A complete Business Profile, clear service pages and genuine reviews improve the experience for people who click your ads and give you visibility that doesn't stop when the budget does.

sections.heading: What the card can't tell you
sections.body_html: The card shows what Google filtered and credited. It doesn't show whether the remaining clicks became customers, whether your landing page converts, or whether your keywords match the jobs you want. Those answers come from your own conversion tracking and records. Treat the card as reassurance about billing, and your lead and sales data as the real measure of whether your ads work.

sections.heading: A monthly ads check for local businesses
sections.body_html:
1. Open the Invalid traffic card and note estimated savings and credited cost.
  2. Check the Invalid clicks column for unusual spikes by campaign.
  3. Compare ad leads with booked jobs or signed clients from your own records.
  4. Review your search terms and add negatives for irrelevant queries.
  5. Test your lead form on a phone to make sure it works and is protected.

sections.heading: Third-party click fraud tools
sections.body_html: Google's help page notes that third-party tools might flag traffic as invalid, such as duplicate IP addresses or bot activity, that Google has already filtered and excluded from your bill. Before paying for a separate tool or filing an investigation, compare its reports with the Invalid clicks column and the new card. If the suspicious clicks are already filtered, you were not charged for them.

sections.heading: The short version
sections.body_html: Google Ads now shows invalid traffic savings and credits in an Overview card. You aren't charged for invalid traffic, but you still need to protect your lead forms and measure real outcomes. Anaheim and Orange County advertisers should check the card, secure their forms and track leads to sales.

faqs.q: What is the Google Ads invalid traffic card?
faqs.a: An Overview page card showing estimated savings from invalid traffic protection and credits for past invalid activity.

faqs.q: Do I pay for invalid clicks?
faqs.a: No. Google says it doesn't charge for invalid traffic; later detections are credited where appropriate and possible.

faqs.q: Why can't I see the card?
faqs.a: Google says it is rolling out gradually and may not be available in your account yet.

faqs.q: Why are credits smaller than filtered clicks?
faqs.a: Filtered clicks are removed before billing; credits only cover activity found after billing.
Its filters can't block traffic from your site, so protect forms with tools like reCAPTCHA and validation.

faqs.q: How far back can I request an investigation?
faqs.a: Google says investigations cover activity within the last 60 days.

faqs.q: How much did Google reduce invalid leads?
faqs.a: Google says by an average of 30% so far in 2026.

faqs.q: Do you work with businesses in Anaheim and Orange County?
faqs.a: Yes. Chimera is based in Anaheim, California and works with businesses across Orange County, California, from Anaheim and Santa Ana to Irvine and the coastal cities.
